tier_reason: First-party (AWS Labs) README screenshots of a cold/warm Lambda load test against Node.js 20 on ARM 128MB; the test function (example/functions/src/v3-lib.mjs) is public but the load-test harness, CPU model and build flags are not, so it falls short of A and there is no independent measurement.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: 'up to over 10x faster startup and up to 2x overall lower cost compared to other JavaScript runtimes running on AWS Lambda'. Screenshots (benchmarks/llrt-ddb-put.png vs benchmarks/node20-ddb-put.png, DynamoDB Put, ARM, 128MB, 64 cold starts, 20000 warm starts): cold-start p50 Lambda-reported Init+Function duration 64.16 ms vs 1511.93 ms for Node.js 20 (about 23.6x, derived from page data); cold-start p50 HTTP round trip 235.61 ms vs 1719.00 ms (about 7.3x, derived from page data); warm p50 14.94 vs 33.20 ms (lambda) and 43.72 vs 62.08 ms (HTTP). The 2x cost claim has no numbers on the page.
corrections.workload: AWS Lambda DynamoDB Put function (example/functions/src/v3-lib.mjs), ARM, 128MB: 64 cold starts and 20000 warm starts, percentiles p0-p100 of Lambda-reported Init Duration plus Function Duration and of HTTP round-trip time; results only as two PNG screenshots in the README.
corrections.caveats: Only first-party numbers, shown as screenshots committed once on 2024-01-31 ('Add perf screenshots') and never refreshed, so they reflect the launch-era LLRT against Node.js 20, not current versions of either. The win is cold start, where a no-JIT QuickJS runtime with a bundled SDK wins by design; warm p50 HTTP latency is only about 1.4x better (derived from page data) and CPU-heavy code would favor V8's JIT. The load-test harness that produced the tables is not in the repo (benchmarks/ holds the PNGs, fetch-streaming.mjs and a v8-v7 suite). The README calls LLRT experimental and 'intended only for evaluation purposes', and says it is not a drop-in Node.js replacement (many node: modules missing, e.g. http, tls, worker_threads). Written in Rust on QuickJS, so it is a runtime to adopt, not a C++ library. The '2x lower cost' claim has no published numbers.

notes: README claim and screenshot numbers verified; tier C stays (vendor first-party, harness not public, no CPU model). Main shortcomings: 2024 screenshots never refreshed, cold-start-only win, experimental and not Node-compatible; metadata (Apache-2.0, 8.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-05, active) checked and correct.

tier_reason: The intro doc gives only prose ranges against interpreted CPython; the project's own tracking suite (mypyc/mypyc-benchmarks code, results in mypyc/mypyc-benchmark-results reports/summary-main.md) states CPython 3.13.1, Ubuntu 24.04.1 and an Intel Core i5-1145G7 but not the C compiler or flags, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: mypyc/doc/introduction.rst: existing code with type annotations is often 1.5x to 5x faster when compiled; code tuned for mypyc can be 5x to 10x faster; compiling all non-test code is how mypy achieved a 4x performance improvement over interpreted Python. The project's automated results page (github.com/mypyc/mypyc-benchmark-results/blob/master/reports/summary-main.md, CPython 3.13.1, Ubuntu 24.04.1, Intel Core i5-1145G7, relative to interpreted Python, at mypy commit 1ca7337 on 2026-10-05): richards 22.36x, spectral_norm 12.91x, hexiom 10.42x, raytrace 9.24x, deltablue 7.86x, bm_float 7.68x, binary_trees 6.34x, nqueens 2.41x.
corrections.caveats: The intro page gives prose ranges only, and the 4x for mypy is the project's own figure with no harness on that page. The tracking suite (mypyc/mypyc-benchmarks, runbench.py) is first-party, covers only 8 benchmarks written for mypyc (e.g. bm_richards_mypyc.py), so its 2.4x-22x reflects tuned code rather than typical annotated code, and it does not state the C compiler or flags. mypyc is a subdirectory of the mypy repository, not a standalone repo, and the docs call it alpha software ('only recommended for production use cases with careful testing'); generated code must be rebuilt per Python release (not abi3). Licence is MIT, with mypyc/lib-rt/pythonsupport.h, getargs.c and getargsfast.c under PSF-2.0 and lib-rt/base64 under a BSD-2-Clause-style licence (all OSI).

notes: Numbers on the intro page match the record; tier C stays. Added the stronger first-party results page (CPU stated, compiler/flags not) to claimed_speedup and caveats; consider it as an alternative benchmark_url. Metadata checked: MIT (PSF-2.0 and BSD portions in lib-rt), 20.7k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, active.

tier_reason: The README 'Performance' chapter has a first-party pystone table against uncompiled Debian Python 2.7 with public benchmark code (tests/benchmarks/pystone.py) and Nuitka flags (--lto=yes --pgo-c), but no C compiler version or CPU model, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README pystone table (pystones/second, best run): Debian Python 2.7 uncompiled 137497.87 vs 460995.20 compiled with LTO (3.353x) and 503681.91 with PGO (3.663x); Nuitka Python 2.7 uncompiled 144074.78 (1.048x) vs 479271.51 LTO (3.486x) and 511247.44 PGO (3.718x). The page's factors are all relative to uncompiled Debian Python 2.7; relative to its own uncompiled run the Nuitka Python 2.7 rows are about 3.33x (LTO) and 3.55x (PGO) (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: The published table is pystone on Python 2.7 only; the README says Python 3 measurements will follow later, and the pystone3 commands it shows have no published results. pystone is a synthetic benchmark. No CPU model and no C compiler version for the table (a separate README section says clang6 beat gcc-6.3 slightly on Linux and MinGW64 beat MSVC by about 20% on Windows). The documented commands contain a typo for the compiled Python 2 run ('sort -n | head -rn 1', head has no -r option) and the text says 1000 runs while that loop runs 100, so the table cannot have come from the commands exactly as printed. An independent timing in the Shed Skin README shows Nuitka 0.6.16 at 11.4 s on the sieve example (n=100000000), identical to CPython 3.11.0 (11.4 s) and only slightly faster than CPython 3.10.6 (13.4 s), so gains on other workloads can be near zero. Licence is AGPL-3.0 with a runtime exception (LICENSE-RUNTIME.txt) covering the compiled output.

notes: Numbers verified in README Performance chapter and Shed Skin independent timing confirmed; the record's 3.49x/3.72x for the Nuitka Python rows are the page's factors against Debian uncompiled, corrected. Tier C stays; metadata checked (AGPL-3.0 with runtime exception, 15.2k stars, develop branch last commit 2026-10-05, active).
